headline: Highest risk is data leakage from Chatwoot’s broad network egress into pdf.js browser-based PDF handling; prompt-injection and capability-conflict are lower because no shared channel is documented.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Chatwoot can ingest external messages and integrations, while pdf.js processes PDF files in a browser-based worker model. No shared channel is documented, so a direct injection path is not proven; however, if Chatwoot content is manually copied into PDFs or browser inputs, prompt-like content could influence downstream handling. Uncertainty keeps this above none.
conditions: IF Chatwoot output is manually pasted into a PDF or browser field consumed by pdf.js
IF an operator treats PDF text as instructions rather than data
mitigations: Use copy/paste only for sanitized excerpts
Render Chatwoot output as plain text, not instructions
Disable any auto-action on PDF text
Add a review step before reusing content
requires-engineering: add provenance labels between systems

B_data_leakage.rationale: Chatwoot touches customer data, contact profiles, interaction history, orders, and messages, and has broad network egress. pdf.js handles PDF files locally with no network egress, so the main leakage risk is Chatwoot exporting sensitive content into PDFs or browser-visible artifacts that pdf.js then opens. This exists in default workflows and can expose sensitive data across work products.
conditions: IF Chatwoot exports customer records or messages into PDF files
IF pdf.js is used to open PDFs containing customer data
mitigations: Restrict PDF exports to redacted fields
Open only approved PDFs in pdf.js
Separate customer-data exports from general document workflows
Turn off unnecessary Chatwoot integrations
requires-engineering: enforce DLP on exported PDFs

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Chatwoot has broad network egress and integration APIs, while pdf.js has no network egress and only file-based PDF input. Their write surfaces do not overlap in the profiles, so direct resource contention is not documented. Any conflict would require an external orchestrator or shared mutable workspace not shown here, so the pathway is limited and uncertain.
conditions: IF both agents are placed on the same writable workspace by an external orchestrator
IF Chatwoot exports files that pdf.js simultaneously reads or rewrites
mitigations: Keep outputs in separate directories
Avoid concurrent writes to shared files
Use read-only mounts for pdf.js inputs
Stagger export and review steps
requires-engineering: add file locking in the orchestrator

D_cascading_error.rationale: Chatwoot produces customer-facing content and reports, and pdf.js can render PDF documents from files. If Chatwoot-generated text is converted into PDFs and then treated as authoritative by pdf.js-based review, errors can cascade without verification. The pair lacks a documented validation boundary, so the safer medium rating is warranted.
conditions: IF Chatwoot-generated content is converted into PDFs for downstream review
IF pdf.js output is accepted without human verification
mitigations: Require human review of generated PDFs
Compare PDF text against source records
Mark generated documents as untrusted
Limit pdf.js use to viewing, not decision-making
requires-engineering: add checksum-based source verification

E_compliance.rationale: Chatwoot touches customer data, contact profiles, interaction history, orders, and messages, which can include regulated personal data. pdf.js handles PDF documents locally and has no network egress, so the compliance issue is not a residency mismatch but a retention and disclosure mismatch if customer data is exported into PDFs. The pair therefore presents a moderate compliance risk.
conditions: IF customer data or messages are exported into PDF documents
IF those PDFs are retained longer than the source records
mitigations: Set a short retention window for exported PDFs
Redact personal data before export
Restrict PDF access to authorized reviewers
Document the export purpose
requires-engineering: align retention policies across systems
